title: Terraform Variables, Locals & Outputs: The Input/Output Handbook
summary: A deep field guide to Terraform's input plumbing — variable declarations, the full type system, validation and lifecycle conditions, tfvars precedence rules, sensitive-value propagation, locals, and outputs. Covers mechanics, trade-offs, and the gotchas that bite in real modules.

chapters.title: Variables: Anatomy & Purpose
points: Input variables are a module's function parameters: they parameterize a config without editing it
Declaration syntax: `variable "region" { type = string, default = "us-east-1", description = "..." }`
Variable names must be unique per module; reserved names disallowed: `count`, `for_each`, `source`, `version`, `providers`, `depends_on`, `lifecycle`, `locals`
Reference syntax is `var.<name>` — never `variable.name`; interpolation `"${var.name}"` is legacy, use bare `var.name`
Meta-arguments a variable block accepts: `type`, `default`, `description`, `validation`, `sensitive`, `nullable`, `ephemeral`
No `default` = required variable; Terraform prompts interactively at plan/apply unless a value is supplied
`nullable = false` rejects an explicit `null` and forces the default to be used instead; default is `nullable = true`
Passing `null` to a variable that has a default means "use the default" — a common source of surprise
Variables are evaluated before any resource; they cannot reference resources, data sources, or other variables
`description` shows in `terraform plan` prompts and is harvested by terraform-docs for README generation
Root-module variables come from the CLI/environment; child-module variables come from the `module` block arguments
Example child call: `module "vpc" { source = "./vpc"  cidr = var.cidr }` — arg names must match declared variable names exactly
Unused declared variables are legal but noise; undeclared values passed to a module are a hard error
`ephemeral = true` (1.10+) marks a value usable during operations but never written to state or plan files

chapters.title: The Type System: Primitives to Structural
points: Three primitive types: `string`, `number`, `bool` — Terraform has one numeric type, no int/float split
Collection types hold many values of ONE type: `list(T)`, `set(T)`, `map(T)`
Structural types hold many values of DIFFERENT types: `object({...})`, `tuple([...])`
`object({ name = string, port = number })` — keys fixed, each with its own type
`tuple([string, number, bool])` — positional, fixed length, per-position types
`any` is a placeholder: Terraform infers a concrete type at call time, it is not a wildcard that skips checking
`optional(string)` inside an object marks a key that may be omitted; it becomes `null` when absent
`optional(string, "http")` supplies a default for the omitted key — much cleaner than `coalesce` downstream
Type conversion is automatic where unambiguous: `"5"` to number 5, `true` to `"true"`, list to set (dedupes and loses order)
Sets are unordered and deduplicated; converting `["a","a","b"]` to `set(string)` yields 2 elements
`map(string)` keys are always strings; a map literal with a non-string key is coerced
Omitting `type` entirely means `any` — accepts anything and defers all errors to usage sites
Type mismatch is caught at plan time with `Invalid value for input variable`, before any API call
Complex default example: `default = { engine = "postgres", version = "15" }` typed as `map(string)`
Trade-off: strict `object(...)` types give early errors and self-documenting modules; `any` gives flexibility and terrible error messages

chapters.title: Validation Blocks & Custom Rules
points: A `validation` block runs a boolean `condition` and shows `error_message` when it is false
Example: `validation { condition = length(var.name) <= 32  error_message = "name too long" }`
Inside `condition` you may only reference the variable itself (`var.this_one`) — no other variables or resources
Multiple `validation` blocks per variable are allowed; all are evaluated and every failure is reported
Regex check: `condition = can(regex("^ami-[0-9a-f]{8,}$", var.ami_id))`
`can(...)` swallows an evaluation error and returns bool — the idiomatic way to test convertibility
`try(a, b, c)` returns the first expression that evaluates without error; used for shape-tolerant lookups
Set membership: `condition = contains(["dev","stage","prod"], var.env)`
Numeric range: `condition = var.port > 0 && var.port < 65536`
Cross-element check with `alltrue([for s in var.subnets : can(cidrnetmask(s))])`
`error_message` must be a full sentence ending with a period (older versions enforced this strictly)
Validation runs at plan time, before providers are consulted — fails fast and free
`precondition` / `postcondition` in a `lifecycle` block validate resource-level assumptions and CAN reference other objects
`check` blocks (1.5+) assert non-blocking conditions and emit warnings instead of failing the apply
Trade-off: validation catches typos early but pushes policy into modules; OPA/Sentinel keeps policy central

chapters.title: Assigning Values & Precedence
points: Six sources, in ascending priority: defaults, `TF_VAR_*` env vars, `terraform.tfvars`, `terraform.tfvars.json`, `*.auto.tfvars` (alphabetical), then `-var-file` and `-var` in command-line order
Later source wins for the same variable name — highest precedence is the last `-var` / `-var-file` on the command line
`terraform.tfvars` and any `*.auto.tfvars` load automatically; other files need an explicit `-var-file=prod.tfvars`
Environment form: `TF_VAR_region=us-west-2 terraform plan` — name is case-sensitive after the prefix
Complex values via env var need HCL syntax in a string: `TF_VAR_tags='{team="core"}'`
tfvars files use plain `name = value` assignments — no `variable` keyword, no expressions referencing `var.`
tfvars files are NOT HCL configuration: no functions, no resources, no interpolation of other variables
`-var 'list=["a","b"]'` works for complex types but quoting rules differ between bash and PowerShell
Terraform Cloud/HCP workspace variables map onto the `-var` level and override tfvars files
`.auto.tfvars` files load in lexical filename order, so `01-base.auto.tfvars` loses to `02-override.auto.tfvars`
Convention: commit `terraform.tfvars.example`, gitignore `*.tfvars` holding secrets
Variable definitions files apply only to the ROOT module; child modules get values only through their `module` block
Missing required variable in non-interactive CI fails with `No value for required variable` — pass `-input=false` to make that explicit
Debug precedence confusion by running `terraform console` and evaluating `var.name` under the same flags

chapters.title: Sensitive Values & Secret Hygiene
points: `sensitive = true` on a variable redacts it from plan/apply output as `(sensitive value)`
Sensitivity is contagious: any expression derived from a sensitive value becomes sensitive too
Sensitive values are still stored in PLAINTEXT in state — redaction is a display feature, not encryption
An output built from a sensitive input must itself declare `sensitive = true` or Terraform errors out
`nonsensitive(expr)` strips the marking — an explicit, auditable escape hatch, never a default move
Sensitive values cannot be used in `count`, `for_each`, or resource identifiers because the plan would leak them
Provider arguments marked sensitive in the schema redact automatically even without your annotation
`ephemeral = true` variables (1.10+) never touch state or plan files at all — stronger than `sensitive`
Write-only arguments on resources (1.11+) accept an ephemeral value that is never persisted
Real secret sources: Vault provider, cloud secret managers, CI-injected `TF_VAR_*` — not tfvars in the repo
State backends must be encrypted at rest and access-controlled; S3 + SSE + strict IAM is the baseline
`terraform output -json` prints sensitive values UNREDACTED — a common accidental CI log leak
Debug logs (`TF_LOG=trace`) can contain secret request bodies; never attach them to public issues
Rotating a leaked value means rotating at the source, not just editing the tfvars file

chapters.title: Locals: Named Expressions
points: `locals { name = expr }` defines named intermediate values — a module's private constants
Reference with `local.name` (singular) even though the block is `locals` (plural)
Locals CAN reference variables, resources, data sources, and other locals — variables cannot
Multiple `locals` blocks per module are allowed and merge into one namespace
Locals cannot be set from outside; they are not part of the module interface
Locals are lazily evaluated and form a DAG — circular references are a plan-time error
Classic use: naming convention, `local.prefix = "${var.project}-${var.env}"`
Classic use: merged tags, `local.tags = merge(var.tags, { ManagedBy = "terraform" })`
Conditional shaping: `local.size = var.env == "prod" ? "m5.large" : "t3.micro"`
Building maps for `for_each`: `local.subnets = { for i, c in var.cidrs : "net-${i}" => c }`
Locals accept no `type`, `description`, or `validation` — type is inferred, documentation lives in comments
Overusing locals hides logic behind indirection; a local used once is often worth inlining
Locals have no runtime cost — they are resolved during graph evaluation, not stored in state
Rule of thumb: variable for what callers choose, local for what you compute from those choices

chapters.title: Outputs: The Return Values
points: `output "vpc_id" { value = aws_vpc.main.id }` exposes a value from a module
Root outputs print after apply and are readable via `terraform output` / `terraform output -json`
Child-module outputs are the ONLY way a parent reads inside that module: `module.vpc.vpc_id`
Output arguments: `value`, `description`, `sensitive`, `depends_on`, `ephemeral`, `precondition`
Outputs are persisted in state, which is how `terraform_remote_state` cross-stack reads work
`depends_on` in an output forces ordering when the dependency is not visible in the expression
A `precondition` in an output block asserts a guarantee before the value is published
Outputs are evaluated after apply; referencing an unknown value during plan shows `(known after apply)`
Removing an output is a breaking change for any consumer reading it via remote state
Cross-stack read: `data "terraform_remote_state" "net" { ... }` then `data.terraform_remote_state.net.outputs.vpc_id`
Prefer explicit narrow outputs over dumping whole resource objects — the whole object leaks fields and churns
`terraform output -raw name` gives an unquoted string for shell piping
Outputs cannot be referenced inside the same module that defines them; use a local instead
Module authoring rule: variables in, outputs out — those two blocks are the module's public API

chapters.title: Variables vs Locals vs Outputs vs Data
points: Variable = input from caller; settable externally; cannot reference anything else
Local = internal computed value; not settable externally; can reference everything in the module
Output = value published to caller or CLI; stored in state; evaluated after apply
Data source = value fetched from a provider at plan time; read-only external lookup
Validation support: variables have `validation`, outputs have `precondition`, locals have none
Sensitivity: variables and outputs take `sensitive = true`; locals inherit sensitivity but cannot declare it
State footprint: variables no (except when embedded in resources), locals no, outputs yes, data sources yes
Typing: variables are explicitly typed, locals and outputs are inferred
Reference prefixes at a glance: `var.`, `local.`, `module.<name>.<output>`, `data.<type>.<name>`
Choose a data source over a variable when the value already exists in the provider and would otherwise be copy-pasted
Choose a variable over a data source when the value is a deliberate choice, not a discovered fact
Choose a local over repeating an expression three times; choose repetition over a local read once
Terraform has no global scope — every module gets values only through its own variables
Anti-pattern: a variable whose value is always computed from another variable; that is a local

chapters.title: Common Mistakes & Gotchas
points: Writing `variable.foo` instead of `var.foo` — the block keyword is not the reference prefix
Expecting `default` to apply when `null` was passed explicitly; it does, and that surprises people expecting `null`
Assuming tfvars supports expressions — `region = var.other` in a tfvars file is invalid
Forgetting that `*.auto.tfvars` loads silently, so a stray file in the directory changes the plan
Losing order by typing a variable `set(string)` when order matters — use `list(string)`
Type `any` on a module input, producing a plan error deep inside the module with no line pointing at the caller
Sensitive input feeding a non-sensitive output: `Output refers to sensitive values` blocks the plan
Committing `terraform.tfvars` with credentials, then rotating nothing after removing it
Using a sensitive or unknown value in `for_each`, which fails with `Invalid for_each argument`
Nesting `optional()` outside an object type — `optional` is only valid on object attributes
Number precision: very large integers can drift because Terraform numbers are arbitrary-precision decimals rendered through JSON
`TF_VAR_` names are case-sensitive; `TF_VAR_Region` does not set `var.region`
Variable defaults that reference the environment (like an AWS account id) — defaults must be constants
Deleting a module output while another workspace still reads it via remote state, breaking that plan silently until next run
Relying on interactive prompts in CI instead of `-input=false`, causing a hung pipeline

chapters.title: Recap: The Input/Output Cheat Sheet
points: Variables parameterize; locals compute; outputs publish — that triad is the whole module interface
Declaration skeleton to memorize: `variable "x" { type, default, description, sensitive, nullable, validation }`
Type ladder: primitives, then `list`/`set`/`map` for homogeneous data, then `object`/`tuple` for shaped data
Prefer a precise `object({...})` with `optional(k, default)` over `any` for every public module input
Precedence order to recite: defaults, `TF_VAR_*`, `terraform.tfvars`, `.tfvars.json`, `*.auto.tfvars` alphabetically, `-var-file`/`-var` last
Validate early with `validation` + `can(regex(...))`; validate against reality with `precondition`/`postcondition`
`sensitive` hides from output; `ephemeral` keeps out of state; neither encrypts the backend for you
Encrypt state, lock it, and restrict access — that is the real secret boundary
`local.` for computed naming, tags, and `for_each` maps; keep resource blocks readable
Outputs are the module's return values and a stable contract — name and version them carefully
`terraform console` is the fastest way to inspect what `var.x` and `local.y` actually resolved to
Ship modules with typed variables, descriptions, validations, and narrow outputs; that is what makes them reusable
Trade-off summary: strict typing and validation cost authoring time but move failures from apply-time to plan-time
The final rule: variables are what callers decide, locals are what you derive, outputs are what you promise
